newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovakia says Czechs failing NATO entry terms.
newsitem.headline: Slovakia says Czechs failing NATO entry terms.

text.p: A rift between Slovakia and the Czech Republic threatened to spill over into the issue of NATO expansion on Wednesday, after the Slovak government accused Prague of failing to meet its international commitments.

In a strongly-worded statement, Slovakia, which is seen as having only an outside chance of being in the first wave of the security alliance's eastward expansion, warned of Czech foot-dragging in the settlement of issues from the breakup of Czechoslovakia in 1993.

The statement, issued by the government of Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar, said Slovakia planned to inform members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation of these failures by the Czechs, widely seen as a leading NATO candidate.
"One of the conditions for NATO membership is the settlement of outstanding problems with neighbours," the statement said.
"We therefore consider it necessary to draw the attention of NATO member states to the fact that the Czech Republic has not fulfilled this condition in relation to the Slovak Republic," it added.

The Czechs and Slovaks have yet to settle numerous divorce issues -- such as the division of federal gold reserves and cultural artefacts, and cross ownership of some banks -- resulting from the split of Czechoslovakia in 1993.
"It (the Czech Republic) does not negotiate, nor does it want to negotiate," the statement concluded.

But the Czech foreign ministry played down the rift in a statement of its own on Wednesday, saying both states had shown the ability to solve "much more difficult and extensive problems than those which have remained open until now".
"The Czech Republic has been and is prepared and willing to resolve all open questions in mutual relations between the two countries."
"(It) is interested in the best relations with Slovakia, to which the content and form and tone of the Slovak government statement surely do not contribute."
The Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary are widely seen as the post-communist countries most likely to be invited to join NATO when the alliance holds its summit in Madrid in July.

Slovakia, roundly criticised by the European Union and NATO countries including the United States for its halting transition to democracy, has lately been left out of official statements on first wave expansion candidates.

Last month President Michal Kovac called a referendum for May on NATO membership at the instigation of the opposition. Parliament, led by the governing coalition, crafted three vaguely-worded questions on the subject, including one on the deployment of nuclear weapons and troops on Slovak soil.
The opposition says the wording of the referendum is phrased to elicit a vote against membership to cover up the government's failure to be included in the first wave.
The referendum pits Kovac against Meciar, avowed political foes. Kovac has accused Meciar of deceiving and misleading the public on the issue, questioning his democratic credentials.
